finding: The take-back buys surface and closes nothing, and this spec supplies the proof. §2.0a says the release "either takes the --check half back or states plainly that it does not close the gap it opens with" and then "It takes it back: --check reads the same predicate as --record". The gap it claims to close is spec/0.46.0.md §8, and §8's diagnosis is role scoping, not severity: "consecutive_clean counts rounds with zero findings across every role" while the shipping rule reads spec_coverage_clean_rounds plus no-FAIL, and §8's own two candidate shapes are converge_roles and a conformance-streak predicate -- neither of which is severity parity. §8 has already been edited to cede the requirement ("which spec/0.37.0.md §2.0a has since taken back into that release"), so no other release now carries it. On the very cycle §8 was written about, parity leaves --check where it was: §2.0a itself records that v0.36.0's rounds 12 and 13 produced error-severity findings, error is blocking, so a parity --check at that cycle's stop still exits 1 -- which is exactly the "never -- no round reaches zero" cell §2.1 gives that cycle. The release therefore adds a --check obligation and a parity test to close a gap it does not touch, and the only release that could have closed it has been emptied.
suggestion: Take back what §8 actually asked for, or take nothing back. If parity is the intent, say plainly that it makes --record and --check agree and does NOT reach §8's role-scoping gap, and restore that requirement to spec/0.46.0.md §8 instead of leaving it owned by a release that cannot satisfy it. Either way, state the v0.36.0 outcome under parity (still exit 1) beside the claim, since the release already has that measurement.

finding: Non-Goal 3 says this release "only reads" severity, but there is nothing that reads the audit vocabulary, and the one shipped reader inverts it. engine.SeverityRank (internal/engine/cluster.go:32-41) maps critical 0, high 1, medium 2, low 3 and returns 4 for everything else, so error, warning and info all rank 4 -- §2's own table says this. The 67 legacy rows §2 counts carry high/medium/low, which that map DOES rank. So the cheap path -- reuse the shipped ranker, as review's merge does at review_merge.go:224 -- orders a legacy low (3) as more severe than a current error (4), and a blocking set written as SeverityRank(s) <= SeverityRank("high") makes every error row non-blocking and every legacy low row blocking. The release needs an audit-vocabulary rank or blocking set in at least two places: §2's clean predicate, and §3's merge fix ("where review's merge keeps the highest severity" -- that comparison does not exist for audit and cannot be added without one). Neither the function, its unknown-value behaviour, nor a test for it appears in §7, so decomposition either invents it twice or discovers the dependency mid-implementation.
suggestion: Name the audit blocking set explicitly in §2 (which of error|warning|info blocks, and what an unrecognised or legacy value does) as a predicate over the audit vocabulary, and state that engine.SeverityRank is the REVIEW ranker and must not be reused. Add one §7 test pinning error blocking, warning/info not, and a legacy high/medium/low row resolving the way §2 says -- otherwise the merge fix in §3 has no comparator to call.

finding: The precondition spends the exact resource the knob exists to save, and Non-Goal 3 has now closed the cheap way to meet it. §2 requires that "before blocking may gate, the severity a row carries must be checkable by something other than the row's author". Non-Goal 3 forecloses the sink ("Any future proposal that makes --record refuse a row is a different release, and this one must gate on what is already recorded or not gate at all"), so the only checker §2 leaves is the one it names itself: severity "is checkable against the finding's own text by a later round". A later audit round is one merged file times every role in the corpus -- under tp run, one subagent process each -- which is the most expensive round-trip tp has. The knob's whole measured value is rounds: §2.1 scores it saving six of nine on v0.35.0. So a gate that must be checked by a round can save at most (rounds saved minus one) and, on the two-clean-rounds rule, must be checked in each round it wants to end. The release ships with the precondition unmet either way: state it and the gate never arms, drop it and blocking gates on a label the release just spent forty lines proving nothing checks.
suggestion: Price the precondition before adopting it. If the only checker is a later round, say what the gate costs in rounds and compare it against §2.1's six-round saving -- that comparison is the release's actual AX case and it is not made anywhere. If the arithmetic does not survive, the honest options are defaulting to all (zero migration, zero new decision for every existing project) or dropping the precondition and stating that blocking gates on an unchecked self-declared label, which is the same objection §2 uses to defer scope a fourth time.

finding: Test 6 still requires an output key the new §4 mechanism has no event for. §4 was rewritten this round into the derived form -- the streak walk stops at the first spec_hash boundary, "zero stored bytes", nothing mutates -- and test 6's second clause survives from the withdrawn stored-reset draft: "resets consecutive_clean to zero AND reports the reset on the machine-readable surface". Under a derived walk there is no reset to report; consecutive_clean simply returns what the walk returns. The payload already carries the boundary: audit --status emits audit_rounds in full (internal/cli/audit_record.go:337-344) and every entry serialises spec_hash (engine.ReviewRound, reviewstate.go:23), beside consecutive_clean, stale and converged. An agent comparing the last two rounds' spec_hash learns the same fact from bytes it is already parsing. A dedicated reset key is therefore a field on every --record and --status response that changes no agent decision, and it arrives with no --compact disposition in a release whose sibling contract (spec/0.31.0.md §8.4, REFERENCE.md:634) requires one for every emitted field.
suggestion: Delete the reporting clause from test 6 and let the test assert the derived value: after a round recorded under a different spec_hash, consecutive_clean is 0 while audit_rounds still shows both rounds with their differing spec_hash. If a signal is genuinely wanted, justify it against the two keys already present rather than adding a third, and give it a --compact disposition.

finding: The audit-side nonblocking_open counterpart is required in a subordinate clause of a corrections paragraph, and the price of that clause is not stated anywhere. The field's ABSENCE from audit is pinned by name in six places: TestReviewNonBlockingOpen_AuditUnaffected (internal/cli/reviewconvergeon_clean_test.go:185-205) asserts audit --record and audit --status never emit it; TestCompact_AuditOmitsHarnessKeepsNextAction (harness_note_test.go:263) repeats it; skills/tp/REFERENCE.md:634 states it in the --compact disposition sentence; skills/tp/SKILL.md documents it as review-only; and spec/0.31.0.md §8.4 plus its numbered test 18 say "nonblocking_open is review-only ... and is never an audit field". So the clause obliges inverting a guard that lives in the review-convergence test file while Non-Goal 4 declares review untouched, and rewriting the two documents every agent reads for the output contract. The new field is not named, has no shape, no emission rule (review emits it only on a clean round with a positive count, so presence itself signals accepted-open), no --compact disposition, and no §7 test. §2.0a notes only that "§7 does not"; the cost of the reversal is what is missing.
suggestion: Either name the field and budget it -- its name, when it is emitted, its --compact disposition, the guard tests and docs it supersedes, and one §7 test -- or drop the surfacing claim and say the remaining rows stay visible in the round file and overlap_report, which are already emitted and cost nothing new.

finding: §3 correctly records that under blocking the order role files reach --merge decides whether a round is clean, and stops one step short of the cost: the agent cannot recover the decision from tp's own output. dedupAuditRows (internal/cli/audit_merge.go:191-211) drops the later row silently and then sorts the survivors by (role, item_id), so the merged file no longer carries the input order that decided the verdict, and --merge reports only duplicates_removed as a bare count (audit_merge.go:59) -- no ids, no roles, no severities. An agent handed a clean round produced by a dropped error row has to re-read every role file to discover it, which is the round-trip --merge exists to remove, and under tp run those files are the only surviving evidence after the authoring subagents have exited.
suggestion: Whatever rule §3 picks for the collision, require --merge to name what it dropped when the dropped row differs from the kept one in status or severity -- ids and severities, not a count. That is a few bytes on the rounds where it matters and absent otherwise, and it is what makes the gate auditable without re-reading the role files.

finding: §3 states a decision as open in the same sentence that closes it. "this release has to pick one, because §7 test 4's nine-round replay is only meaningful under live recomputation" -- and §7 test 4 is normative in this release, as is test 5 ("A row dispositioned wontfix or duplicate is excluded from the finding count"), which is unwritable against a clean flag stamped at record time. So the document already contains its answer: live recomputation. Leaving the choice open buys a decomposition question, an escalation candidate under tp run, and a review round on a decision the spec has made in its own test section -- in a release whose §2.1 asks decomposition to treat one default as contested and whose §5 argues that length is this repository's strongest measured predictor of cycle cost.
suggestion: Write the choice into §3 as a sentence: audit cleanliness is recomputed live from the recorded rows under the resolved audit_converge_on, matching review_status.go:91, and the stored clean flag becomes a record-time artifact no consumer reads. Then §7 tests 4 and 5 are acceptance rather than the place the decision hides.

finding: The saving §5 claims has been spent and then some, and it is measurable from this spec's own snapshots. Line counts: spec/.tp-review/0.37.0/snapshot-round-1.md 287, snapshot-round-2.md 229, the current text 306. §5's removal of three sections bought 58 lines in round 2; rounds 2 and 3 of repair prose put 77 back, so the file is now 19 lines LONGER than the 288-line draft whose length was the entire argument for the removal, and it has crossed the 300-line mark CLAUDE.md records as the boundary between roughly 8-9 total rounds and roughly 23. §5 still asserts the saving in the present tense. Almost all of the 77 lines are archaeology of drafts no implementer will ever see: §2's "An earlier draft of this section claimed" plus its four-point refutation, "the first attempt at building it was withdrawn in the round after it was written", §2.1's "The 1-1 split this paragraph used to rest on is withdrawn", §2.0a's "Two corrections this sentence needed, both from round 2". This is precisely the class spec/0.43.0.md §2 measures -- findings sitting in text the previous round had just written -- and every remaining round pays it once per role.
suggestion: Apply §5's own rule to the repairs. Keep the surviving requirement of each corrected passage and move the refutation history to spec/0.35.0-candidates.md or a 0.37.0 candidates file, where the reasoning is read once by whoever reopens the question rather than by every role in every round. Re-measure after the edit: if the file is not back under the round-1 count, the length argument in §5 should be deleted rather than left asserting a saving the document no longer has.

finding: Self-caught, recorded per this round's instruction. Having measured snapshot-round-1.md at 287 lines and snapshot-round-2.md at 229, I was about to report that §5's "The three added ~100 of 288 lines" is false because the removal is worth 58 lines, not ~100. That would have been my arithmetic error presented as the spec's: 58 is the NET delta of a round that removed the three sections and simultaneously added the §5 removal notice and the §2 refutation list, so a ~100-line removal and a 58-line net delta are consistent. The claim as written is about how much the three sections occupied, and nothing I measured contradicts it. The finding that survives is the different one filed above -- the file is now longer than the 288 the argument was made against -- and it needed the same three numbers read correctly.
suggestion: No spec change. Transferable rule for this loop: a net line delta is not a section size, and a spec's own snapshots are the only artifact that can tell them apart.

finding: Self-caught. My first form of the severity-ranker finding was that tp ALREADY mis-ranks audit rows, because engine.SeverityRank returns 4 for error|warning|info while legacy audit rows carry high|medium|low. Checking every caller before writing it: SeverityRank is called from review_merge.go:224, cluster.go:90 and locationcluster.go:117 -- all review paths -- and dedupAuditRows (audit_merge.go:191-203) compares nothing at all, so no audit path ranks a severity today and there is no shipped defect. The correct claim is the forward-looking one: the inversion is what the release WILL buy if it reuses the shipped ranker, which is the cheap path and the one §3's "where review's merge keeps the highest severity" points an implementer at. Filed that way. The wrong version would have been a code-defect claim in a spec review, refutable in one grep.
suggestion: No spec change beyond the filed row. Recorded because the wrong version would have read as stronger evidence than the right one.
